opus-5.5.text:
I think the pressure really depends on where a team sits relative to the critical path. At OpenAI, some teams are directly on the path to the next model launch: pretraining, post-training, the infrastructure that training runs depend on. When you're on one of those teams, the pressure is very concrete. There's a deadline, a lot of compute is committed, and if something breaks at two in the morning, someone has to fix it, because every hour the cluster sits idle is very expensive. So the pressure there isn't someone standing behind you with a whip. It comes from the situation itself. You know that what you're doing is blocking a lot of other people.

Other teams are more exploratory, doing research whose payoff might come six months or a year later. The pressure there is a different kind. It's less about "this must ship next week" and more about "am I working on the right thing, and will this matter?" That can be stressful in its own way, because there's no clear signal telling you whether you're making progress.

The culture is also fairly bottom-up. Nobody really micromanages your hours. But the people around you are extremely strong and very self-driven, so you naturally hold yourself to that bar. A lot of the pressure is self-imposed. You see what your colleagues are getting done, and you want to pull your weight.

Personally, I think the healthiest way to see it is that the pressure is proportional to how much leverage your work has. If you're on a team where your code is used by everyone training models, a small mistake gets amplified, but so does a good improvement. I actually find that motivating. You just have to learn to pace yourself, because it's a marathon, not a sprint. The people who burn out are usually the ones who treat every week like a launch week.

r002.rationale: The response mentions pacing and exploratory work with longer-term payoffs, but does not present getting infrastructure reconstruction right over time as a reason to tolerate delay.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and honestly the answer is that it varies a lot, probably more than people outside would guess.

When I was there, I'd say the pressure mostly tracked how close you were to the product and the launch cycle. Teams that were directly on the critical path for a release, things like the API, serving infrastructure, the stuff that actually has to be up when millions of people hit it, those teams felt it the most. If there's a launch coming and your component isn't ready, there's nowhere to hide. And once something is live, you're also carrying on-call, incidents, scaling problems that show up at 2am. That's a very different kind of stress from research stress.

On the research side, the pressure was more self-driven. Nobody's standing over you saying ship by Friday, but you're surrounded by extremely strong people, and the bar you set for yourself just naturally goes up. There's also this feeling that the field is moving so fast that if you don't push, your direction might get overtaken in a few months. So it's less deadline pressure and more existential pressure, if that makes sense.

Then there's a middle layer, which is where I spent a lot of my time, the training infrastructure and RL systems work. That one's interesting because you're serving both sides. Researchers want things yesterday so they can run experiments, and at the same time if your system has a bug, you might waste a huge amount of compute, which is very expensive. So the pressure there is about correctness and throughput more than about external deadlines.

The other thing I'd say is that the intensity is somewhat lumpy. There are crunch periods before a big model or product release where basically everyone's pulled in, and then calmer stretches. Different teams hit those peaks at different times, so if you only looked at one snapshot you'd get a misleading picture of who's working hardest.

And honestly a lot of it comes down to the manager and the team culture. Two teams with the same workload can feel completely different depending on whether the lead protects people's time or just passes pressure downward. That was true at OpenAI the same way it's true anywhere.

r001.rationale: The response does not compare post-training with Jiayi Weng’s infrastructure-reconstruction team or attribute greater pressure to post-training’s explicit deadlines. It says infrastructure work is pressured by correctness and throughput.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that infrastructure reconstruction should be done right over the longer term or that this justifies tolerating delay.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between how much work a team has and what makes that work stressful. One team might feel pressure from deadlines and dependencies; another might feel it from uncertainty—working hard without knowing whether an approach will succeed. Those are different experiences, even if the hours look similar.

I don’t have enough visibility to rank teams across OpenAI. I’d want to understand how clear their priorities are, how much control people have over their work, and whether they can recover after an intense period. Those things can matter as much as the workload itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the amount of work from the kind of pressure. A research team might feel pressure from uncertainty: you can work hard without knowing whether an approach will succeed. A product or infrastructure team might face more immediate pressure from deadlines, reliability, and issues affecting users.

I wouldn’t assume every team at OpenAI has the same experience. The stage of a project, how priorities are set, and how a manager handles tradeoffs can all make a big difference. So I’d look beyond hours and ask: Are expectations clear? Can people prioritize? And after an intense period, do they have time to recover?
